title: The Best Pour-Over Coffee Setup for Home
dek: The exact dripper, kettle, and scale to brew café-style pour-over in your kitchen, at three budgets.
intro: Pour-over is how most specialty coffee bars show off a single-origin coffee: hot water, a paper filter, and control over every step. At home it's cheap to start and hard to master, and the gear decides which part is hard.
You need three things: a dripper, a gooseneck kettle (for a slow, aimed pour), and a scale. Skip the scale and you're guessing. Skip the gooseneck and you're flooding the bed.
how_we_picked: We built around the tools coffee bars already use for pour-over, then added value alternatives. Specs are from the Amazon listings.

picks.verdict: The cone most cafés use. Cheap, ceramic, nothing to break down. It rewards good technique.
The same V60 with 100 filters, so you can brew the day it shows up. Easy gift.
Brews and serves in one beautiful vessel. Thick filters, very clean cup.
Precise temperature and a pour you can steer. The premium pick.
Temperature presets and keep-warm for a fraction of the price.
1L capacity for full Chemex brews, still affordable.
0.1g accuracy and a built-in timer. The cheapest upgrade with the biggest payoff.

bar_tip: Start at a 1:16 ratio (for example 20g coffee to 320g water), water just off the boil, about 3 minutes total. Too sour? Grind finer. Too bitter? Grind coarser.

faq.a: V60 for one or two cups and more control; Chemex for brewing a pot to share and a cleaner, lighter cup.

faq.q: Do I need a gooseneck kettle?
faq.a: For pour-over, yes. A regular kettle dumps water too fast to control extraction.
Any burr grinder from our grinder guide. The Baratza Encore is the easy default.
